    88	\begin{remark}[Line answers as coefficient lists]
    89		\label{rem:deg-line-representatives}
    90		The source refers to the elements of $\deg_{md}(\ell)$ as polynomials
    91		``defined on the line $\ell$'', that is, as functions on the point set
    92		of $\ell$, while its decision procedure expects each line answer as a
    93		list of coefficients. The two readings differ. When $md \geq q$,
    94		distinct coefficient lists induce the same function $\F_q \to \F_q$;
    95		and when $\ell$ has direction $v = 0$ --- a case the question
    96		distributions produce with positive probability
    97		(Remark~\ref{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}) --- the point set of $\ell$ is
    98		the singleton $\{u_0\}$, so a function on $\ell$ retains only a single
    99		field element of the answer. Definition~\ref{def:ideg-deg-polynomials}
   100		therefore adopts the coefficient reading, under which the strategy's
   101		line measurements are indexed by exactly the answers of the prescribed
   102		form, and its evaluation convention reproduces the universal
   103		quantification of the line-versus-point clauses of the win predicates
   104		(Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate}).

   127	\begin{definition}[Commuting and anticommuting tuples]
   128		\label{def:anticommuting-tuple}
   129		% The quantity gamma is introduced in the source at eq:gamma-value, inside
   130		% the completeness analysis of the Pauli basis test; that label has no
   131		% corresponding node here, so the definition below is self-contained.
   132		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:subfield-trace}
   133		For a tuple
   134		$\omega = (u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z) \in (\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$, let
   135		\[
   136			\gamma(\omega) \,=\, \tr\big( (r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)) \cdot (r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)) \big)\,,
   137		\]
   138		where $r_W \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_W)$ is the scalar multiple of the
   139		vector $\mathrm{ind}_m(u_W) \in \F_q^{M}$, the middle $\cdot$ is the
   140		$\F_q$-inner product of two vectors in $\F_q^{M}$, and
   141		$\tr = \tr_{q \to 2}$. The tuple $\omega$ is called \emph{anticommuting}
   142		if $\gamma(\omega) \neq 0$, and \emph{commuting} if $\gamma(\omega) = 0$.
   143	\end{definition}
   144	
   145	The sign $(-1)^{\gamma(\omega)}$ is exactly the sign with which the
   146	generalized Pauli observables $\tau^X(r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X))$ and
   147	$\tau^Z(r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z))$ commute
   148	(see Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-commutation});

   151	\begin{lemma}[Probability of anticommuting tuples]
   152		\label{fact:omega-anticomm-prob}
   153		% The source states this result in a `fact' environment; fact environments
   154		% become lemma nodes and the paper label is kept verbatim.
   155		% The exact value of the anticommuting probability and the constant lower
   156		% bounds under the hypothesis m <= q are additions relative to the source,
   157		% which asserts only the two bounds displayed at the end of the statement;
   158		% the source states those bounds without the hypothesis m, d >= 1, under

   160		% unconditional constant bounds are what the proof of the lemma labelled
   161		% lem:qld-win-implications uses.
   162		\uses{def:anticommuting-tuple}
   163		A tuple $\omega = (u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)$ sampled uniformly at random from
   164		$(\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$ is anticommuting with probability exactly
   165		\[
   166			\big(1 - q^{-1}\big)^{m+1} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\,,
   167		\]
   168		and commuting with the complementary probability, which is at least
   169		$\frac12$. In particular, if $m \leq q$, then $\omega$ is anticommuting
   170		with probability at least $2^{-4}$ and commuting with probability at
   171		least $\frac12$. If $m, d \geq 1$, then the probability that $\omega$ is
   172		anticommuting is at least
   173		\[
   174			(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot \Big(1 - \frac{md}{q}\Big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}

   176		\]

   178		$\big(1 - \frac{3md}{q}\big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$.

   856	\begin{definition}[Symmetric equivalents]
   857		\label{def:symmetric-equivalents}
   858		\uses{def:expanded-state}
   859		For the remainder of this chapter, as well as in
   860		Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining}, the six registers
   861		$\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'\mathsf{A}''\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'\mathsf{B}''$
   862		are partitioned into two ``parties'' in two different ways. The first
   863		scheme takes $\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'$ as one party and
   864		$\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''$ as the other; the second scheme takes
   865		$\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'$ as the first party and
   866		$\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''$ as the second. Thanks to the symmetry of the
   867		Pauli basis test under exchanging the two players, and the symmetry of
   868		the ancilla states in registers $\mathsf{A}'\mathsf{A}''$ and
   869		$\mathsf{B}'\mathsf{B}''$, every bipartite consistency relation of the
   870		form
   871		$M_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx_\delta N_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$
   872		derived below also yields, by the same derivation with the registers
   873		appropriately changed, the three relations
   874		\[
   875			N_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx_\delta M_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,,\qquad
   876			M_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'} \approx_\delta N_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''}\,,\qquad
   877			N_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'} \approx_\delta M_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''}\,.
   878		\]
   879		Similarly, every single-party relation of the form
   880		$M_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx N_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}$ also
   881		holds on the register pairs $\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''$,
   882		$\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'$ and $\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''$. These variants
   883		are called the \emph{symmetric equivalents} of the derived relation.
   884		Several lemmas below conclude by asserting that all symmetric
   885		equivalents also hold, and later chapters invoke exactly these
   886		variants.
   887	\end{definition}

blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:44:	The symmetrization argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-strat} below invokes Naimark dilation in the form of Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark} (stated and proved in Chapter~\ref{chap:projective}): a bipartite state together with two sub-measurement families can be replaced, without changing any of the correlations $\bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^y_b \ket{\psi}$, by a product-extended state together with projective sub-measurements on the enlarged spaces. When the input families are complete measurements, the dilated projective sub-measurements can be completed by assigning the residual projector of each family to one fixed outcome; the resulting projective measurements reproduce the same correlations on the extended state, since the correlation-preservation identity forces the extended state to lie in the range of the total projector of each dilated family. This completed form, with genuinely projective measurements, is the one used in Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-strat}; for the proof the source refers to Theorem 5.1 of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}, which is stated for complete measurements. The source follows its statement of the dilation theorem with a sentence announcing an ``orthogonalization lemma'' from the literature that is never actually stated there; nothing in this chapter depends on it.
blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:132:	The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-strat} yields, for each $\eps' > \eps$, a symmetric projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps'$. The conclusion as stated, at $\eps' = \eps$, does not follow from this: the dilated dimension $d$ may grow as $\eps' \downarrow \eps$, and the supremum defining $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G)$ in Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-value} need not be attained by any strategy. The symmetrization construction itself is value-preserving, so the conclusion does hold whenever the hypothesis supplies an actual strategy of value at least $1-\eps$ rather than only the value of the game; every use of the lemma in the source proceeds from such a strategy, or from a strict lower bound on the value, and therefore consumes only what the proof establishes. The gap and the available repairs are documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_symmetrization-attainment}.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:108:	The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, and the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} shows that any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount, which is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.

The proofs require the latter reading, $H = \F_q$, which is adopted throughout this chapter: the linearity of $\mathrm{Dec}$ and the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g_h) = h$ for all $h \in \F_q^{M}$, both of which fail for the boolean map, are used in the symmetry step of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} and in the conjugation identity \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6}. Every encoding satisfies it, because then $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)} = g$ as polynomial representatives; a polynomial that is not an encoding need not: for $m = 1$, $d \geq 2$, and $q > 2$, the polynomial $g(x) = x^2$ has $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_1(u) = u$, which differs from $g(u) = u^2$ at every $u \notin \{0,1\}$. blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:9:This chapter completes the analysis of the Pauli basis test~\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. Throughout, $(q,m,d)$ is an admissible parameter tuple (Definition~\ref{def:admissible}), $q = 2^t$, and $M = 2^m$ denotes the number of $q$-ary qudits tested for per player. (The letter $M$ also denotes measurement operators, always carrying super- and subscripts; the meaning is determined by context, as in the source.) blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:6:This chapter defines the two testing primitives underlying the question-reduction step: the \emph{classical low individual degree game}, in its simultaneous form, and the \emph{Pauli basis test}, a nonlocal game built from the classical game together with the Magic Square game. blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:6:This chapter defines the two testing primitives underlying the question-reduction step: the \emph{classical low individual degree game}, in its simultaneous form, and the \emph{Pauli basis test}, a nonlocal game built from the classical game together with the Magic Square game. The chapter closes with the qubit form of the soundness statement (Corollary~\ref{cor:pauli-binary}) and the canonical parameter choice with its soundness bound (Definition~\ref{def:introparams}, Lemma~\ref{lem:delta-bound}).
blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:164:	The two-prover tensor-code test for the code $\code^{\ot m}$, as described in Figures~1 and~2 of~\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, agrees with the game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ with parameters $\mathsf{ldparams}$ and $k=1$ on every question pair whose diagonal-line direction is nonzero: the axis-parallel line-versus-point test is their axis-parallel lines test, with the roles of the two players chosen uniformly at random, which is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor-code test from Section~4.1 there; the diagonal line-versus-point test is their subcube commutation test, again with the added symmetrization between the players; and the consistency test is their synchronicity test. blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:256:The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:370:	with $\gamma$ as in Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value}: the two measurements commute when $\gamma = 0$ and anticommute when $\gamma = 1$. If $\gamma = 0$, define $E^{\mathsf{Pair},\omega}_{\beta_X,\beta_Z} = A_{\beta_X} B_{\beta_Z}$ and $E^{(\mathsf{Pair},X),\omega}_a = A_a$, $E^{(\mathsf{Pair},Z),\omega}_a = B_a$, and let the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ and $\mathsf{Variable}$ measurements be trivial (identity on the all-zeros outcome). If $\gamma = 1$, let the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ and $\mathsf{Variable}$ measurements be those produced by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac} from the anticommuting consistent pair $(A, B)$, acting on the auxiliary $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$ factor, and let the $\mathsf{Pair}$ measurements be trivial. The strategy is symmetric and projective by construction; every measurement is either a post-processed Pauli basis measurement, a measurement supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, or (in the $\gamma = 0$ case) a product of two commuting consistent measurements, so the strategy is consistent, and commutativity along every edge of $G^{\mathrm{pauli}}$ is checked case by case --- for instance, $(\mathsf{Point},X)$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_1$ commute because both are $X$-basis measurements. Consistency and projectivity give the consistency checks with certainty, and the low-degree checks pass because the answers agree with the strategy determined by the polynomial $g_h$ in the classical game. For the remaining checks: when $\gamma = 0$ the commutation check passes by construction, and when $\gamma = 1$ the Magic Square check passes by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}; the consistency checks 5 and 7 pass with certainty because $\tau^W_{[\tr(g_\cdot(y)\, r_W) = \cdot]} \ot I$ coincides with $E^{(\mathsf{Pair},W),\omega}$, respectively with the embedded $\mathsf{Variable}_1$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_5$ measurements of Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac} (item~3 there). Hence the strategy has value $1$.

It relies on the classical soundness theorem (Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}) and on the rigidity of the Magic Square game (Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-rigidity}).

- [ ] F1 (blocker) `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:164` — `lem:ld-soundness` relies on a false identity between the seeded line/polynomial game and the cited ordered-pair tensor-code game.

## Review

Changes are required. F1–F3 leave cited theorem applications unproved.

**F1.** The source proof of `lem:ld-soundness` calls the games “identical” and invokes Theorem 4.7 immediately at [08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex](/Users/dengnifer/Documents/ghz/ldt/MIPStarRE-dev/.worktrees/issue-0002-qpbt-blueprint/references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:447), lines 447–454. But [Ji et al., Figure 1, Definition 4.5, Figure 2, and Theorem 4.7](https://arxiv.org/html/2111.08131) use a hidden subcube, send an ordered pair `(u,v)`, and receive two field values. The blueprint instead sends a seeded diagonal line and receives a polynomial. Its nontrivial cross-tests also have mass `2/9`, versus `1/3` in the cited game. A valid reduction must construct pair measurements by postprocessing, handle hidden subcubes and seed fibers while preserving projectivity and synchronicity, and prove the resulting value bound, approximately `rej_tensor ≤ 3/2 rej_ld + O(1/(mq))`. The claimed difference of only `2/(mq)` does not establish this.

**F2.** The same provider theorem requires its auxiliary parameter `K ≥ 12mt`. For the degree-`d` Reed–Solomon code, `t = d+1`, but line 164 takes `K=m³d`, which can be smaller than `12m(d+1)`. Taking `K ≥ max(m³d,12m(d+1))` and redoing the polynomial/exponential error absorption would repair this source-hypothesis omission.

**F3.** The QPBT mirror at [14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex](/Users/dengnifer/Documents/ghz/ldt/MIPStarRE-dev/.worktrees/issue-0002-qpbt-blueprint/references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:713), label `thm:linearity`, inserts `δ≤1`; [Natarajan–Vidick Theorem 10](https://arxiv.org/html/1610.03574v1) does not. Lines 233–241 then apply the restricted version separately to each `(x,z)`, although a small global average does not imply every conditional defect is at most one. Import the provider statement without this restriction, or supply an explicit good/bad-fiber saturation argument before averaging.

**F4.** The cited proof of Facts 4.13–4.14 at [05_quantum_preliminaries.tex](/Users/dengnifer/Documents/ghz/ldt/MIPStarRE-dev/.worktrees/issue-0002-qpbt-blueprint/references/neexp-paper/05_quantum_preliminaries.tex:420), lines 420–428, uses `A_a²≤A_a` and `B_a²≤B_a`, giving “at most twice” the off-diagonal mass. Equality is stated only for projective measurements. Replace “leaves exactly twice” accordingly.

**F5–F6.** The divisibility note currently treats removal of the seed as the only game-format mismatch. Its directly indexed game still reveals an index and asks for a polynomial, unlike the cited pair measurement, and its verdict therefore overstates the proposed repair. Moreover, averaging each prover’s line measurement separately changes a seeded synchronicity correlation `E_s⟨M_s⊗N_s⟩` into `E_{s,s'}⟨M_s⊗N_{s'}⟩`; Naimark dilation preserves the latter, not the former. The note must give a faithful source comparison and a transport that actually controls all cross and synchronicity branches.

**F7.** `rem:qld-4-13-source-defects` correctly observes that the source statement at [14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex](/Users/dengnifer/Documents/ghz/ldt/MIPStarRE-dev/.worktrees/issue-0002-qpbt-blueprint/references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1020), label `lem:qld-4-13`, claims `poly(m²ε,md/q)`, while lines 1134–1137 prove only `m·poly(ε,md/q)` and lines 1241–1245 use an unsupported joint-law decomposition. Under [policy.tex](/Users/dengnifer/Documents/ghz/ldt/MIPStarRE-dev/.worktrees/issue-0002-qpbt-blueprint/docs/paper-gaps/policy.tex:19), lines 19–33 and 121–129, this requires a separate self-contained note and citation.

**F8.** That policy also requires blueprint bibliography entries to carry published URLs at lines 248–252. The comment claiming an `EVOLUTION.md` override has no corresponding protocol entry, while `texra-blueprint.toml` still defines the published site base. Both new entries should use their configured published note URLs.

   455		the projector $\Id$ minus the sum of each dilated sub-measurement to
   456		have zero mass on the extended state. Finally, since the auxiliary
   457		state is a product state, a unitary acting on each player's ancilla
   458		qubits alone carries it to $\ket{0 \cdots 0} \ot \ket{0 \cdots 0}$;

   460		preserves projectivity and all correlations. The success probability
   461		of a strategy is a linear combination of its correlations, weighted by
   462		the question distribution and the win predicate
   463		(Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-value}), and is therefore
   464		unchanged.
   465	\end{proof}

   752	\section{Expanding the Hilbert space and defining commuting observables}
   753	\label{sec:expanding}
   754	
   755	The next step of the analysis adjoins ancillary EPR registers to the
   756	players' state and lifts the strategy observables and measurements to the
   757	expanded state. The point of the construction is that the ancilla factor of
   758	each lifted observable carries the \emph{exact} Pauli commutation sign, so
   759	that the signs cancel and the lifted observables approximately commute for
   760	every tuple $\omega$.
   761	
   762	\begin{definition}[Expanded state]
   763		\label{def:expanded-state}
   764		\uses{def:projective-strategy-setup, def:EPR}
   765		Recall that $M = 2^m$. Introduce registers $\mathsf{A}', \mathsf{A}'',
   766		\mathsf{B}', \mathsf{B}''$, each with Hilbert space isomorphic to
   767		$(\C^q)^{\ot M}$, and define the state
   768		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-psihat}
   769			\ket{\hat{\psi}}_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'\mathsf{A}''\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'\mathsf{B}''}
   770			\,=\, (\ket{\psi})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}}
   771			\ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}_{\mathsf{A}'\mathsf{A}''}
   772			\ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}_{\mathsf{B}'\mathsf{B}''}\,,
   773		\end{equation}
   774		where $\ket{\psi}$ is the extended strategy state of the strategy
   775		under analysis (Lemma~\ref{def:projective-strategy-setup} and the
   776		convention following it) and
   777		$\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ is the maximally entangled state on
   778		$\C^q \ot \C^q$ (Definition~\ref{def:EPR}). For the remainder of this
   779		chapter, as well as in Chapters~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining}
   780		and~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction}, all approximations $\approx$ and
   781		$\simeq$ are evaluated with respect to the state $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$,
   782		unless stated otherwise.
   783	\end{definition}
   784	
   785	\begin{definition}[Expanded observables]
   786		\label{def:expanded-observables}
   787		\uses{def:strategy-observables, def:expanded-state, lem:twisted-commutation}
   788		For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $r \in \F_q$, and $u \in \F_q^m$, define the
   789		observable
   790		\begin{equation}\label{eq:lc-23}
   791			\hat{W}^r(u) \,=\, W^r(u) \ot \tau^W(r \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u))\,,
   792		\end{equation}
   793		where $W^r(u)$ is the strategy observable of~\eqref{eq:qld-strat-obs}
   794		and $\tau^W(r \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u))$ is the generalized Pauli
   795		observable acting on $(\C^q)^{\ot M}$, introduced in
   796		Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}
   797		(see Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-commutation}). As a product
   798		of two observables with eigenvalues $\pm 1$ acting on disjoint
   799		registers, $\hat{W}^r(u)$ is itself an observable with eigenvalues
   800		$\pm 1$. If $W^r(u)$ is viewed as acting on register $\mathsf{A}$, then
   801		$\hat{W}^r(u)$ is viewed as acting on registers
   802		$\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'$, with the $\tau^W$ factor acting on
   803		$\mathsf{A}'$. The registers are generally indicated by subscripts, as
   804		in $(\hat{W}^r(u))_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}$ or
   805		$(\hat{W}^r(u))_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$, the latter having the
   806		strategy factor on $\mathsf{B}$ and the Pauli factor on
   807		$\mathsf{A}''$.
   808	\end{definition}
   809	
   810	\begin{definition}[Expanded point measurements]
   811		\label{def:expanded-point-measurement}
   812		\uses{def:expanded-observables, lem:pauli-observable-expansion, def:low-degree-encoding, def:subfield-trace}
   813		For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $u \in \F_q^m$ and $a \in \F_q$, define
   814		\[
   815			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \,=\, \E_{r \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(ar)} \, \hat{W}^r(u)\,,
   816		\]
   817		and define the projector
   818		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qld-point-obs-def}
   819			\tau^{W,u}_a \,=\, \tau^W_{[g_\cdot(u) = a]}
   820			\,=\, \sum_{h \in \F_q^{M} \colon h \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = a} \tau^W_h\,,
   821		\end{equation}
   822		where $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ are the joint eigenprojectors of
   823		the generalized Pauli $W$-observables
   824		(see Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-observable-expansion}).
   825		Expanding both tensor factors of $\hat{W}^r(u)$
   826		by~\eqref{eq:qld-strat-obs} and by the Fourier expansion of the
   827		generalized Pauli observables
   828		(see Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-observable-expansion}), and
   829		averaging over $r$, gives the equivalent convolution form
   830		\[
   831			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a
   832			\,=\, \sum_{\substack{a',a'' \in \F_q \\ a' + a'' = a}}
   833			M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{a'} \ot \tau^{W,u}_{a''}\,.
   834		\]
   835		In particular each $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ is a projection
   836		and $\{\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\}_{a \in \F_q}$ is a projective
   837		measurement.
   838	\end{definition}
   839	
   840	\begin{definition}[Trace-coarse-grained point projections]
   841		\label{def:expanded-point-trace-projection}
   842		\uses{def:expanded-point-measurement, def:expanded-observables, def:subfield-trace}
   843		For fixed $u \in \F_q^m$, $r \in \F_q$ and $b \in \F_2$, define the
   844		projection
   845		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qld-def-mptur}
   846			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u,r}_b \,=\, \sum_{a \in \F_q \colon \tr(ar) = b} \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\,,
   847		\end{equation}
   848		which can be equivalently written as
   849		\begin{equation}\label{eq:lc-22}
   850			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u,r}_b \,=\, \frac{1}{2} \Big( \Id + (-1)^b\, \hat{W}^r(u) \Big)\,.
   851		\end{equation}
   852		The register conventions are those of
   853		Definition~\ref{def:expanded-observables}.
   854	\end{definition}

   877			N_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'} \approx_\delta M_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''}\,.

   880		$M_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx N_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}$ also
   881		holds on the register pairs $\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''$,
   882		$\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'$ and $\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''$. These variants
   883		are called the \emph{symmetric equivalents} of the derived relation.
   884		Several lemmas below conclude by asserting that all symmetric
   885		equivalents also hold, and later chapters invoke exactly these

   680	 \subsection{Combining the $X$ and $Z$ measurements}
   681	\label{sec:combining}
   682	
   683	In this section our goal is to create a set of combined measurements
   684	that simultaneously measure the approximately-commuting measurements
   685	constructed in the previous section. We do this first for the points.
   686	Recall that $\mH_\alice$ and $\mH_\bob$ denote the Hilbert spaces corresponding to
   687	registers $\alice$ and $\bob$, respectively.
   688	
   689	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:qld-4-10}
   690	There exists a function $\delta_Q(\eps) = \poly(\eps)$ such that the following holds. 
   691		For every $x,z \in \F_q^m$ and $\mH \in \{ \mH_\alice, \mH_\bob\}$ there are projective measurements $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}_{a,b \in \F_q}$ acting on $\mathcal{H} \otimes (\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$ such that:
   692		\begin{enumerate}
   693			\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) On average over uniformly random $x,z \in \F_q^m$,
   694			\begin{equation}
   695				\label{eq:qld-q-self-cons}
   696				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'}  \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\bob \alice''}\,.
   697			\end{equation}
   698			
   699			\item (\textbf{Consistency with $\hat{M}$}) On average over uniformly random $x,z \in \F_q^m$,
   700			\begin{gather}
   701				\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-xz}
   702					(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x}_{a} \hat{M}^{(\Point,Z),z}_b)_{\bob \alice''}\;, \\
   703								\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx}
   704					(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{M}^{(\Point,Z),z}_b  \hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x}_{a} )_{\bob \alice''}\;.
   705			\end{gather}
   706	              \end{enumerate}
   707	                    Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations
   708	      also hold.
   709	\end{lemma}
   710	
   711	The construction of the measurements $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}$ whose existence is guaranteed in the lemma proceeds in three steps. In the first step, for every $(r,s)\in\F_q^2$ we combine the binary-outcome measurements $\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x,r}_a$ and $\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),z,s}_b$; this is made possible by their approximate commutation as shown in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons}. In a second step, we show that the measurements thus constructed have a particular ``approximate linearity'' property, when seen as a function of the pair $(r,s)$. This allows us, in the third step, to combine them into a single measurement $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}$ with outcomes in $\F_q^2\cong \F_2^{2t}$ by applying the following  result from~\cite{NV17}:
   712		
   713		\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test]
   714		\label{thm:linearity}
   715			Let $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, let $t$ be a positive integer, and let $\ket{\psi}$ be a state in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_\alice \otimes \mathcal{H}_\bob$. Suppose that on average over $u, u'$ chosen uniformly from $\F_2^t$, we have the following ``approximate linearity'' holds:
   716			\[
   717	(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'})_{\alice} \approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^{u+u'})_{\alice}
   718			\]

1	# Blueprint Style Guide & Lessons Learned
     2	
     3	## Core Philosophy
     4	The blueprint is a **bridge between the mathematics and the Lean formalization**. A reader should be able to read a blueprint entry and immediately understand the corresponding Lean declaration. Conversely, someone reading the Lean code should find the blueprint proof sketch faithful to what the code actually does.
     5	
     6	## General Principles
     7	1. **Blueprint ↔ Lean must match.** Every `\lean{X}` tag must correspond to an actual Lean declaration. Every proof sketch must match what the Lean proof actually does — not a hand-wavy version of it.
     8	2. **Standalone.** `blueprint/` and any slides are independent — no cross-references, no shared files. Each has its own macros, its own `references.bib`.
     9	3. **Mathematical language only — zero Lean jargon.** No Lean identifiers in prose (no `selfImprovement_step`, no `PastingLemma.aux`, no `rintro ⟨X, hX⟩`). The `\lean{...}` tag is the link; the body text is standard mathematics. If you can't say it in math, rewrite it.
    10	4. **No filler prose.** Only precise definitions, theorem statements, and proof sketches. No "this is important because..." or "the self-improvement step governs the induction...".
    11	5. **Cite non-trivial things.** Basic definitions don't need citations. Important results and non-obvious definitions should cite the source paper.
    12	6. **Don't invent terminology or notation.** Don't create ad-hoc notation when standard notation exists. Don't name things that the literature doesn't name.
    13	7. **Match Lean's theorem/lemma/def exactly.** If Lean says `theorem X`, use `\begin{theorem}`. If Lean says `lemma X`, use `\begin{lemma}`. `\begin{proposition}` is allowed in blueprint prose when it improves mathematical readability, but still map it to an actual Lean `theorem`/`lemma` declaration via `\lean{...}`. Label prefix: `thm:` for theorem, `lem:` for lemma, `def:` for definition, `prop:` for proposition.
    14	
    15	### Remark On Mathematical Prose
    16	
    17	Blueprint entries should read as mathematical exposition, not as progress
    18	reports. The mathematical argument should determine the order of the prose:
    19	introduce the notation, state the assertion, give the proof or calculation, and
    20	then record Lean references through the usual blueprint tags. Lean declarations,
    21	file paths, and proof-status information should not become the visible structure
    22	of the paragraph. When referring to a source article, cite it bibliographically
    23	rather than relying on an uncited reference to the article.
    24	
    25	Use displayed formulae when the formula benefits from visual separation, and
    26	keep short scalar definitions or elementary inequalities inline when the
    27	sentence reads better that way. As in ordinary mathematical writing, displayed
    28	formulae should be punctuated as part of the sentences in which they occur.
    29	
    30	## Proof Sketches Must Match Lean
    31	This is the most important rule. Every proof in the blueprint must faithfully describe what the Lean proof does:
    32	
    33	- **Reference the actual lemmas used.** If the Lean proof calls `LDT.selfImprovement`, the blueprint proof should say "By Lemma X.Y (self-improvement)..." and list it in `\uses`.
    34	- **Do not use `\cref` or `\Cref`.** The blueprint does not load `cleveref`.
    35	  Spell out the kind of object and use ordinary references, for example
    36	  `Lemma~\ref{lem:self-improvement}` or `Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}`.
    37	- **Describe the actual proof structure.** If Lean does induction on a parameter, say so. If Lean uses a specific decomposition, name it.
    38	- **Don't hand-wave where Lean is specific.** "Standard argument" is not acceptable if Lean uses three specific lemmas. Name them.
    39	- **Don't be more specific than Lean.** If Lean uses `simp` to close a goal, a one-line sketch is fine.
    40	- **`\uses` in proofs must be accurate.** Only list what the proof actually uses, not what the statement mentions.
    41	
    42	## Source-Labelled Statements And Conditional Helpers
    43	
    44	If a blueprint theorem, lemma, or proposition carries a source label from the
    45	paper, the linked Lean declaration must state the same theorem, up to faithful
    46	formal encoding of the paper's domain.  Do not use `\lean{...}` and `\leanok`
    47	on the source-labelled statement to point to a conditional helper whose
    48	additional assumptions supply an unproved part of the paper proof.
    49	Changing the Lean statement away from `references/ldt-paper/` is strongly
    50	discouraged unless faithful formal encoding or a documented mathematical
    51	necessity requires it; the blueprint should make any such necessity explicit.
    52	
    53	Boundary hypotheses such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
    54	positivity of parameters, and denominator nonvanishing may be faithful when
    55	they express the mathematical domain that the paper leaves implicit.  By
    56	contrast, bridge inputs, residual data, repair hypotheses, producer
    57	assumptions, proof-obligation inputs, or package assumptions are proof debt.
    58	They must not be added to a source-labelled theorem statement.  If such data is
    59	still unproved, the source-labelled Lean theorem should keep the source-shaped
    60	statement and carry a tracked `sorry`, or the missing assertion should appear
    61	as the lowest named internal obligation with a tracked `sorry`.  A separately
    62	named conditional helper should not be introduced as a repair pattern.  If one
    63	already contains substantial proof content, it may remain temporarily only as
    64	quarantine: it needs a paper source, a tracking issue, and a discharge or
    65	deletion plan.  The blueprint should leave the paper theorem unmarked as
    66	proof-complete until the source-faithful Lean statement has a source-faithful
    67	proof.
    68	
    69	If a Lean theorem proves only a restricted version of a source theorem, the
    70	blueprint entry carrying `\leanok` must state that restriction in the theorem
    71	statement itself.  It must not be cited as the unrestricted source theorem.
    72	When the only Lean declaration available for a source label has extra
    73	non-paper assumptions, remove the `\leanok` claim from the source-labelled
    74	entry or move the restricted statement to a separate Lean-only entry.  The
    75	unrestricted paper theorem remains unformalized until a Lean statement with
    76	the source's hypothesis set exists.
    77	
    78	## Notation Consistency
    79	Notation must be **internally consistent** across the entire blueprint and **close to what the Lean code expresses**:
    80	
    81	- **Indices**: 0-indexed where matching `Fin n` in Lean
    82	- **Finite fields / alphabets**: use standard notation for the alphabet $\Sigma$ and finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$
    83	- **Measurements**: use standard quantum measurement notation (projective measurements, POVMs)
    84	- **Strategies**: quantum strategies for nonlocal games should use standard notation from the literature
    85	- **Expansion**: use standard notation for graph expansion parameters
    86	- **Macros** (in `macros/common.tex`): define project-specific macros and use them consistently
    87	
    88	The original reference controls notation whenever it gives a usable convention.
    89	If the blueprint needs a different symbol, index convention, or name in order to
    90	match Lean, introduce it explicitly and relate it to the paper notation in the
    91	same paragraph.  Do not let a `\lean{...}` tag, a Lean namespace, or a file name
    92	be the only explanation of a changed term.
    93	
    94	When a public Lean declaration is a formalization-only auxiliary lemma, the
    95	blueprint should say so before listing the declaration.  The surrounding prose
    96	should identify the paper theorem, equation, or construction that the auxiliary
    97	lemma supports, and should avoid making the auxiliary name look like a named
    98	result from the source article.
    99	
   100	## What NOT to Put in the Blueprint
   101	- **Lean identifier names in math text.** Write "the self-improvement lemma", never "the `selfImprovement` step". The `\lean{LDT.selfImprovement}` tag handles the linking.
   102	- **Implementation details.** Don't say "bundled as an element of the Euclidean space" or "using `EuclideanSpace.equiv`". Describe the mathematical object.
   103	- **Ad-hoc notation.** Don't invent superscripts or subscripts to distinguish from existing notation. Use standard conventions.
   104	- **Function-call syntax.** Use mathematical notation, not programming notation.
   105	- **Redundant definitions.** If two blueprint definitions describe the same mathematical object, consolidate them. Each definition should introduce genuinely new mathematical content.
   106	- **Lean namespace prefixes in prose.** Don't write "the `LDT.PastingLemma`" — write "the pasting lemma".
   107	
   108	## Banned AI/Software Language (enforced in both blueprint AND Lean code)
   109	The blueprint reads as a **mathematical document**, not software documentation. The following patterns are banned in ALL reader-facing text (section titles, theorem names, proof sketches, remarks, chapter preambles) and in ALL Lean docstrings, comments, and section names:
   110	
   111	### Banned terms → replacements:
   112	| Banned | Use instead |
   113	|--------|------------|
   114	| "Assembly" (as section/chapter title) | "Proof of [theorem]", "Construction", "Composition" |
   115	| "Pipeline" | "reduction", "construction", "proof chain" |
   116	| "Bridge" (as noun for a connection) | "connection", name by mathematical content |
   117	| "Handoff" / "hand off" | "transition", "continuation", or drop entirely |
   118	| "In this blueprint" / "Within this blueprint" | "here", "in what follows", or omit |
   119	| "Honest" (as adjective for rigorous) | "exact", "faithful", "unconditional", "complete" |
   120	| "Glue layer" | "intermediate construction", "connecting results" |
   121	| "Re-export" / "reexport" | "provides", "re-states" |
   122	| "Wiring" / "wire up" | "connecting", "composing", "combining" |
   123	| "Package" (as noun for a data bundle) | "form", "data", "structure" |
   124	| "Sorry-free" | acceptable only in Lean-specific technical context |
   125	
   126	### Additional rules:
   127	- **Section names in Lean**: use mathematical terms (`section QuantumSoundness`, `section SelfImprovement`, `section PastingLemma`), not organizational terms (`section Assembly`, `section Pipeline`).
   128	- **Internal LaTeX labels** (e.g., `\label{ch:soundness}`) are not reader-facing and need not be renamed if doing so would break cross-references. But NEW labels should follow the standard.
   129	- **Definitions that are actually theorems**: if a statement asserts a mathematical fact, it must be `\begin{theorem}`, not `\begin{definition}`. Definitions introduce new objects; theorems prove properties.
   130	
   131	## `\uses` Dependency Guidelines
   132	- **Statement `\uses`**: list only what's needed to *state* the result (typically definitions of the objects involved). Keep minimal — transitive deps are automatic.
   133	- **Proof `\uses`**: list only what the proof *actually calls*. Don't list definitions unless the proof unfolds that definition.
   134	- **Never self-reference**: a proof's `\uses` must NOT include the label of the theorem it proves.
   135	
   136	## Recording Formalization-Only Lemmas
   137	Some Lean lemmas are genuine proof infrastructure rather than named statements
   138	from the original papers. These must be traceable without making the blueprint
   139	look as if the paper stated them.
   140	
   141	- If a declaration directly formalizes a paper or blueprint statement, record
   142	  it as usual with `\lean{...}` on that statement and cite the relevant source.
   143	- If a public declaration is an auxiliary lemma introduced only for the Lean
   144	  proof, make that status explicit. Its Lean docstring should say that it is a
   145	  formalization-only auxiliary lemma and should name the nearby paper equation,
   146	  line range, or blueprint result it supports.
   147	- If such an auxiliary declaration is important enough to be referenced from
   148	  the blueprint, give it a clearly subordinate blueprint node, for example
   149	  `[Formalization support for ...]`, and state in the first sentence that the
   150	  lemma is not a named statement of the paper but isolates a step used in the
    60	- the scope in which the replacement should be used.
    61	
    62	A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
    63	where future readers can learn it.
    64	
    65	Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
    66	should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
    67	rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.
    68	
    69	## Naming Norm
    70	
    71	Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
    72	conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
    73	assembled.
    74	
    75	Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
    76	`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
    77	uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
    78	such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
    79	clearer phrase.
    80	
    81	This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
    82	Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
    83	blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
    84	mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
    85	number, or implementation history.
    86

    93	assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
    94	paper or blueprint would recognize.

## Review

F4 is the substantive mathematical issue. For the admissible tuple \((q,m,d)=(8,1,8)\), take \(g(x)=x^8\). This polynomial representative is not multilinear and hence is not an encoding, but \(\mathrm{Dec}(g)=(0,1)\), so
\[
\mathrm{Dec}(g)\cdot\mathrm{ind}_1(u)=u=u^8=g(u)
\]
for every \(u\in\mathbb F_8\). Thus the claim that the identity “holds exactly when \(g\) is an encoding, and fails otherwise” is false. Line 20’s assertion that the two sides are distinct as functions is false for the same reason. State instead that \(g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}=g\) as polynomial representatives exactly for encodings, while their induced functions may agree for nonencodings when \(d\ge q\).

For F1, the source defines `\game` as `\mathfrak{G}` and consistently uses it for the low-degree, Magic Square, and Pauli games. Chapter 13 uses `\mathcal G`, Chapter 14 uses bare `G`, and Chapter 16 returns to `\mathfrak G`; bare \(G\) also conflicts with the notation for type graphs. Standardize the games as \(\mathfrak G^{\mathrm{ld}}\), \(\mathfrak G^{\mathrm{MS}}\), and \(\mathfrak G^{\mathrm{Pauli}}\), reserving \(G\) for graphs.

For F2, the source’s `\nqubits` expands to \(M\), and Chapters 13 and 16 likewise use \(M=2^m\). Either use \(M\) throughout Chapter 14 or explicitly introduce \(n=M=2^m\) and identify \(M\) as the source notation.

   126	### Additional rules:
   127	- **Section names in Lean**: use mathematical terms (`section QuantumSoundness`, `section SelfImprovement`, `section PastingLemma`), not organizational terms (`section Assembly`, `section Pipeline`).
   128	- **Internal LaTeX labels** (e.g., `\label{ch:soundness}`) are not reader-facing and need not be renamed if doing so would break cross-references. But NEW labels should follow the standard.
   129	- **Definitions that are actually theorems**: if a statement asserts a mathematical fact, it must be `\begin{theorem}`, not `\begin{definition}`. Definitions introduce new objects; theorems prove properties.

   132	- **Statement `\uses`**: list only what's needed to *state* the result (typically definitions of the objects involved). Keep minimal — transitive deps are automatic.

## Review

F1 should separate the definition of “symmetric equivalents” from the assertion that one relation implies the other three. The latter is a mathematical result and should be a lemma with the symmetry argument as its proof. Update the references at `ch15:42`, `ch16:9`, and `ch16:183`, which currently call this definition a remark, together with the associated dependency labels.

For F2, rename the new label to `lem:projective-strategy-setup` and update every `\ref` and `\uses`. The legacy-label exception does not apply to a chapter introduced by this PR.

For F3, state the register structure exactly: each of \(\mathsf A'\), \(\mathsf A''\), \(\mathsf B'\), and \(\mathsf B''\) is an \(M\)-qudit register isomorphic to \((\mathbb C^q)^{\otimes M}\). For F4, replace “the players’ original registers” with “registers \(\mathsf A\mathsf A'\) (respectively \(\mathsf B\mathsf B'\)),” matching the construction at line 61 and the paper.

F5–F7 are direct dependency omissions. Add `def:pauli-win-predicate`, `def:povm-distance`, and `def:expanded-observables` to the respective proof-level `\uses`.

For F8, drop “The lemma keeps the label …; earlier revisions recorded …”; the preceding source-location comment already supplies the useful provenance. For F9, replace “Projectivization of the strategy under analysis” with “Reduction to a projective strategy.”

The sole Lean link, `MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.postprocess`, matches the fiber-sum POVM definition, and its statement-level `\leanok` is valid.
